text: ,14 Amiodarone may also be used;12-14 it has a slower onset but is equally effective17 and is particularly useful in pa- tients with structural heart disease.13 Evidence is more limited for quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide, and sotalol. Adjunctive pharmacological therapy may be started before electrical cardioversion to increase the success of the procedure and to reduce the risk of early recurrence;13,14 drugs used include amiodarone, flecain- ide, ibutilide, propafenone, and sotalol. Once sinus rhythm has been achieved, long-term main- tenance drug therapy needs to be considered since re- lapse is common. Patients with a first episode of atrial fibrillation are rarely started on maintenance therapy, particularly if a reversible cause has been identified and can be treated.13,14 However, patients who have trouble- some symptoms due to paroxysmal or recurrent atrial fibrillation are usually given long-term antiarrhythmics. Drugs used are similar to those used for cardioversion, and again there is limited evidence to guide choice.18 Beta blockers may be tried initially,13 particularly in pa- tients with lone atrial fibrillation,14 and they have the ad- vantage of providing rate control if relapse occurs, but flecainide, propafenone, or sotalol are often required. Amiodarone and dofetilide may also be used; amiodar- one may be more effective than other antiarrhythmics19 but its use is limited by long-term adverse effects and it is generally only recommended in resistant cases or in patients with heart failure who are unsuitable for alter- native therapy. Catheter ablation procedures (for exam- ple, isolation of the pulmonary veins20) are an alterna- tive to drugs, and surgery or implantable defibrillators may be used in selected cases. Patients with infrequent episodes of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation and good re- sponse to drugs may be prescribed single doses of fle- cainide or propafenone for outpatient use (‘pill-in-the- pocket’) if symptoms recur.13,14,21 The choice between rate and rhythm control has been de- bated. Rhythm control has theoretical advantages since restoration of sinus rhythm should both alleviate symp- toms and reduce thromboembolic risk. However, the ad- verse effects and limited efficacy of antiarrhythmic drugs in preventing relapse may limit any benefit. A review22 and meta-analyses23,24 of studies comparing rate control with rhythm control found little difference between the two strategies in terms of symptom control or clinical events, and choice therefore depends on patient character- istics and preference.12-14,25 For elderly patients with min- imal symptoms rate control is generally the preferred op- tion, whereas younger patients or those who remain symptomatic despite rate control should be considered for rhythm control.
